newsitem.title: USA: U.S. markets make Fed March rate hike "disappear".
newsitem.headline: U.S. markets make Fed March rate hike "disappear".

text.p: U.S. financial markets performed a magic trick in late April and May -- they made the Federal Reserve's March interest rate hike disappear.

Initially, U.S. Treasuries and stocks fell, corporate bond spreads widened, and the dollar hit a more than 4-1/2 year high against the yen after the Fed raised the federal funds rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 percent on March 25.
But since then, asset markets have made a spectacular comeback and the dollar has tumbled.

"This is kind of a mystery to me. Given that people do understand that the Fed typically moves sequentially, why do people seem to think the Fed is done before it turns out they are?" St. Louis Fed economist William Emmons told Reuters.
"Maybe it's just the tendency of brokers to be eternal optimists," he quipped.
Others were quick to note that the Fed has never changed the direction of monetary policy and moved rates only one time. The March move was the first rate rise in more than two years.

Yesterday the three major U.S. stock indices -- the Dow Jones Industrials average, the Standard & Poor's 500 and the Nasdaq -- all finished well above their closing levels of March 24, the day before the rate hike.

Also, the 30-year Treasury bond ended below its March 24 yield of 6.92 percent, the three-month to 10-year yield curve had not significantly flattened, and the dollar hit a 4-1/2 month low of 114.70 yen in trade overseas.
And spreads of high-yield corporate bonds have once again narrowed to exactly where they were on March 24, as measured by the Merrill Lynch 175 index.
The index showed spreads of BB- to CCC-rated corporates had returned to a 330-basis-point spread over the 10-year Treasury after widening to 358 basis points by April 15.

Martin Fridson, high-yield global strategist at Merrill Lynch and Co Inc, said new issuance has been so strong recently that last week alone the dollar amount of new debt sold matched the average monthly flow last year, which was a record year.

Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan questioned the aggressive pricing of corporate bonds back in February when he said to a Senate panel, "This optimistic attitude has become especially evident in quality spreads on high-yield corporate bonds -- what we used to call junk bonds."

However, economists who believe the Fed will raise rates again at next Tuesday's Federal Open Market Committee meeting said strong consumer spending, not asset valuations, will be the deciding factor. But as Greenspan said himself, the two are symbiotic.

"Indeed, econometric models suggest that the more than $4.0 trillion rise in equity values since late 1994 should have had a larger positive influence on consumer spending than seems to have actually occurred," he said in his February remarks.
Ken Bercuson, chief economist at SBC Warburg in New York, said changes in consumer spending lag interest rate moves by nine to 12 months, and final demand is not especially interest-rate sensitive.
"A 25-basis-point increase isn't going to have any effect on anything," Bercuson said, referring to the March rate rise.
"I think (Greenspan) is worried about the stock market and I think he is worried these yields are leading to spending levels which are uncomfortable," he said.
